what_it_does: Quantum computers are error-prone: the quantum bits (qubits) they use to store information are exquisitely sensitive to noise, and tiny disturbances cause computation errors. Quantum error correction (QEC) is the technique of encoding one logical qubit of reliable information across many physical qubits so that errors can be detected and fixed. However, these error-correction schemes require qubits to interact with many neighbors (dense connectivity), while today's real quantum hardware only allows each qubit to interact with a few nearby neighbors (sparse connectivity). Mapping a QEC scheme onto sparse hardware currently requires painstaking manual redesign for every combination of error-correction code and hardware layout. QECC-Synth automates this by using a technique called ancilla bridging — inserting extra helper qubits that act as relay stations to implement the needed long-range interactions — and formulating the choice of where to place those helpers as a MaxSAT problem (a combinatorial optimization that finds the assignment satisfying the most constraints). A solver then finds a near-optimal layout automatically for any QEC code and any hardware connectivity graph, without requiring human redesign.
